name: Napster
blurb: The 1999 file-sharing app that shook the music industry until courts shut it in 2001
title: What Happened to Napster? The 1999 Music App and Its Shutdown
description: Napster was the peer-to-peer music-sharing service launched in June 1999. Sued by record labels, it shut down in July 2001; the brand lived on until 2026.
answer: Napster was a free program launched on June 1, 1999, by Shawn Fanning and Sean Parker that let people swap MP3 music files directly between their computers. Record labels, through the RIAA, sued it for copyright infringement in December 1999, and after a court ordered it to block copyrighted songs, Napster shut down its network in July 2001 and went bankrupt in 2002. The name was then sold and reused for a legal paid music service, which ended in January 2026 when its owner turned Napster into an AI company.

body: Napster was a small desktop program. You typed in a song or an artist, it searched a central index of the music files that other users were sharing, and the file came straight from another person's computer. That peer-to-peer design, combined with the new, compact MP3 format, made it feel as if almost any song was a search away, for free and without the artists' or labels' permission.

It spread fastest on college campuses with fast connections; on some campuses it was reported to take up as much as half of all internet bandwidth. Verified use peaked at about 26.4 million users worldwide in February 2001, and unofficial estimates put registrations as high as 80 million.

What happened
rows: Napster launches on June 1; in December, A&M Records and other labels sue through the RIAA
Metallica sues in April after an unreleased song circulates on the network; Dr. Dre files a similar suit
A judge orders Napster to remove copyrighted songs in March; in July it shuts down its network for good
Napster files for bankruptcy in June; in November Roxio buys the name and logo for $5.3 million
Napster returns in October as a legal paid download and streaming store
The brand passes to Best Buy, Rhapsody (which renames its service Napster in 2016), MelodyVR, Hivemind and Algorand, and Infinite Reality
In early January the streaming service is switched off and Napster rebrands as an AI company

body: Napster lost in court, but it showed how many people wanted any song, instantly, on a computer, years before legal download stores and streaming offered that. After it closed, other file-sharing networks without a central index, such as Gnutella and later BitTorrent, took its place. Musicians were split: Metallica said it had identified 335,000 users sharing its songs, while artists such as Chuck D of Public Enemy and Dave Matthews took a friendlier view.

The original file-sharing network has been gone since 2001. The Napster name survived for over two decades as a licensed subscription music service, but in January 2026 that service stopped streaming and the company relaunched as an AI products business under Infinite Reality. Reports at the time said some labels and artists were still owed royalties from the old service.

ul: Waiting a long time for a single song to finish over a slow connection
Files labeled with the wrong artist or title
Metallica, a band many fans loved, suing a service those same fans used
Colleges complaining that Napster traffic was clogging their networks

faq.a: Courts found it was enabling copyright infringement. Under an injunction to block copyrighted songs, which it could not do reliably, Napster shut its network in July 2001.
Shawn Fanning, then a college student, and Sean Parker launched it on June 1, 1999.

faq.q: Is Napster still a music service?
faq.a: No. The paid Napster streaming service ended in January 2026, when its owner Infinite Reality turned the brand into an AI company.
